extracted.intended_audience: academics and clinicians who perform peer review for journals (especially health professions education and biomedical journals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing constructive, collegial, and useful peer review reports for journal manuscripts — balancing feedback for authors with evaluative signals for editors. Focuses on wording, scope, tone, and practical strategies reviewers should apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize multiple aims and audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Write each section of your review with a clear sense of which of the review’s aims and audiences you are prioritizing (service to the field, the journal, or the authors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review serves three aims: uphold shared standards (field), assess potential contribution (journal), and support authors to meet standards and advance the conversation (authors). Explicitly decide whether a comment is for the editor (assessment) or for the author (improvement) and craft wording accordingly. Example: open with a few overall-impression sentences aimed at editors to indicate weight of concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make feedback specific and actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective feedback should be specific and actionable rather than vague.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague dismissals like 'There is a vast literature on this topic that the authors have ignored.' Instead, name missing citations where possible or give concrete instructions (e.g., 'return more clearly in the Discussion to the issue of patient-centred care and how this study challenges its core principles'). Provide examples of problematic passages and suggest exact changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat feedback-forward parts as a conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing authors, write as though you were sitting down with them: build rapport and intimacy to make feedback more acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using first- ('I') and second-person ('you') pronouns can reduce distance and defensiveness. Example contrast: avoid 'The authors do not sufficiently explain themselves…' and prefer 'I stumbled over some of the jargon in your Methods section; I’d suggest…' Use this approach for feedback intended to help the authors revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target the task not the person
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct critique at the manuscript/product rather than at its authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid personal swipes ('The authors seem oblivious…'). Reframe to focus on the work ('The paper’s claim to originality is weakened by its lack of reference to similar work…'). This reduces face-threatening language and increases receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hedging to soften face-threatening judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Hedging (linguistic moves expressing caution/uncertainty) helps save face for authors and reduces reviewer arrogance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modifiers and personal epistemic phrases ('I struggle', 'I’m not persuaded', 'rather uncritical') to indicate opinion rather than absolute truth. Hedging does not mean avoiding necessary critique; it frames critique to maximize uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear signals to editors about weight of concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the editor understands how much weight you assign to concerns and the rationale for your recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with overall-impression lines for the editor (e.g., 'The authors have done a rigorous piece… I find it a compelling piece that represents a novel contribution…'). Use the confidential comments box only to flag ethical/methodological concerns or to contextualize uncertainty, and avoid contradicting public review content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hit the high points; avoid nitpicking
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize major, substantive issues rather than enumerating every minor error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High points include whether the problem matters, methods are appropriate and well-conducted, the story is coherent, and the work is situated in the literature. Do not drown authors in typos and formatting errors; instead give a brief summary about language with a few representative examples if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish reflections from requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate your reflections (brief impressions showing engagement) from concrete revision requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep reflections brief to avoid long, unfocused reviews; demarcate sections so authors know what to respond to. Focus most effort on actionable requests for more, less, or different material in specific parts of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit time and streamline reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of the time you spend; long, exhaustive reviews can indicate overstepping the reviewer role and contribute to burnout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider taking an hour to read and note, pause, then up to another hour to write the review. If it regularly takes much longer, streamline comments and focus on essential issues; you are not the authors’ supervisor or thesis advisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t police — avoid requesting new studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not request that authors conduct another study or fix issues that cannot be addressed via revision at this stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish fixable problems (clarify writing, explain methods) from fatal design flaws (poor study design, low response rates) and honestly indicate when flaws are dealbreakers. Do not fixate on peccadillos that are not fatal to the paper’s contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware your ego and be cautious with self-citation requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using peer review to promote your own work or protect your turf; self-citation requests are common and may be inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you think an omitted citation is central, explain why and provide the citation; do not expect authors to guess. If you cannot engage impartially because you feel personally invested or threatened by the paper, consider recusing yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify yourself thoughtfully (open peer review considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signing reviews changes rhetorical position and may improve tone, but has power implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying yourself encourages diplomacy but may disadvantage early-career reviewers when commenting on senior authors. Be aware of journal policies and power dynamics when choosing to sign reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the confidential/editor-only box appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve confidential comments to the editor for issues that cannot be raised publicly (e.g., ethical concerns) and do not contradict public review content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors rely on consistency between public comments and confidential notes; avoid using confidentiality to hide critiques you didn’t put in the main review. Use the box to clarify weighting or flag sensitive concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from other reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: When journals share other reviewers’ reports, use them as educational resources to refine your own reviewing style and judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading other reviews shows different interpretations and effective phrasing you can adopt. Sharing reviews increases accountability and offers models for balanced critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance positives and critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Include both strengths and weaknesses so critiques are contextualized and not overwhelmingly negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin or balance sections with positive statements (e.g., 'While this Introduction is well written…') and then explain concerns. Balanced phrasing helps editors see nuance and helps authors accept critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be directive when appropriate about content placement and argument
rubrics_metrics.description: When the manuscript fails in structural or argumentative aspects, give clear, directive suggestions about what to change and where.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if the Discussion fails to revisit an Introduction concept, explicitly request returning to that issue and suggest how it could be reframed to show the study’s contribution.
